description:
We're Quantum Foam, an English-Speaking team interested in physics, astronomy, space science and scientific exploration. For NASA Space Apps Ankara, we're exploring the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, aiming for an interactive tool for investigating infrared sky observations and moving objects.

We're looking for teammates with skills in Python, programming, data analysis, astronomy, image processing, UI/UX design and scientific research. People with interest and curiosity are welcome!
summary: Cosmic Echo is a web tool that makes it easy to see how real SPHEREx images of the sky change over time. Users choose one of the five challenge targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) or enter ICRS coordinates, set a field size and detector, and play date-ordered cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA like a short movie. This helps people notice possible motion or brightness changes by eye, the same way Pluto was found, without handling FITS files. It uses SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 data, shows up to five representative weekly frames with pan and zoom, and tells the user when the archive is busy. It does not detect or classify objects automatically. It is a human-guided exploration tool built to make SPHEREx data approachable for the public.
details:
What it does

Cosmic Echo lets anyone inspect SPHEREx observations without handling astronomy file formats. Users pick a challenge target or enter ICRS RA/Dec, then choose a field size and a detector array. The app queries NASA/IPAC IRSA's Simple Image Access service for SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 observations, retrieves FITS cutouts, and shows up to five representative weekly frames in a date-ordered timeline with playback, pan and zoom in Aladin Lite. If the archive is busy or returns an error, the app shows a notice instead of failing silently.

How we built it

We first prototyped the data pipeline in Python (Astropy, astroquery, reproject) to learn the FITS structure, WCS coordinates and the wavelength range of each detector. We then built the web app with Next.js, React and Aladin Lite and hosted it on Vercel. The interface was designed in Figma.

What we learned, and the limits

The six detector arrays (D1 to D6) are not the 102 spectral bands, so frames should be compared within one detector. SPHEREx pixels are about 6 arcseconds, so even a fast-moving star such as Barnard's Star shifts only a pixel or two per year. Our own centroid test was too crude to claim a measured motion, so the tool does not claim detections. It supports human inspection and does not detect or classify objects automatically. Not yet implemented: spectral-band selection, image co-addition or subtraction, Gaia/WISE overlays and contamination flags.

Intended impact

To make SPHEREx data approachable so more people can look for moving and variable objects.

Use of AI

Claude (Anthropic) and GitHub Copilot helped write and debug code and helped draft this text. The team chose the design and approach, reviewed the code and tested the results.
